rv.q: Most impressive are Coombes’ and Essiedu’s astonishing physicality and bravura performances portraying multiple characters through switching accents and mannerisms with convincing ease.
Essiedu has astonishing poise, bringing tragic depth and integrity to Delroy but lilting joy and comedy, too.
Of the two plays, Michael has more visual stimulus in the form of witty props magicked from hidden panels beneath the cross or plucked from ledges on the balconies.

Yet greatly as I admired the unflagging energy of Coombes and Essiedu, I emerged from these plays feeling as though I had been buried under a mountain of words that didn’t say quite as much as they intended to.
Watching Michael unravel in the close confines of @sohoplace is a visceral experience; it’s like being strapped to a rocket powered by fury.
But his unmodulated firing-on-all-cylinders-attack-from-all-sides method results in a scorched earth rather than a clinical strike and clean kill.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this punchy state-of-the-nation trilogy exploring race and class in Brexit Britain through fierce monologues, with critics praising its urgent themes and powerhouse performances while some find the approach uneven.
